notes: Slot 4 = Communist Party of Kazakhstan (Kunaev). Kunaev's patronage clan in 13, KGB in 7, Sredmash (Semipalatinsk, Ulba, BN-350) in 15 as the industrial power bloc, Virgin Lands sovkhoz directors in 14, SADUM in 10, SAVO (HQ Alma-Ata since 1969) in 22 with Baikonur mentioned. MD sprites show post-1991 organizations, so icons are null.

0.name: Milli Türkistan Birlik Komitesi
0.text:
The National Turkestan Unity Committee is the Munich-based émigré body led by Veli Kayum Khan, who headed the German-sponsored Turkestan committee during the Second World War and rebuilt it in West Germany after 1945. On 1 January 1970 it survives as a small exile circle, publishing the journal Milli Türkistan and lobbying Western governments on behalf of Soviet Central Asia's Muslims.

It demands a single independent Turkestan from the Caspian to the Chinese border, governed by a strong national leadership and anchored firmly in the Western camp. Its leverage is thin: contacts in Bonn, Ankara and American cold-war institutions, and the hope that Kazakh listeners of Western radio still honour the memory of Mustafa Shokay.

1.name: Istanbul qazaqtary
1.text:
The Kazakhs of Istanbul are the survivors of the Xinjiang Kazakhs who fled Chinese communism between 1949 and 1951, crossed the Himalayas into Kashmir and were resettled by Turkey in 1952-1954, above all in the Zeytinburnu district. Their elders and the religious scholar Halife Altay keep the community together in 1970, far from Alma-Ata but listening closely to news from the steppe.

They stand for faith, family, the clan and the Kazakh language, and regard Soviet rule as a godless occupation. Firmly anti-communist and loyal to NATO Turkey, they hope for a Kazakhstan that is Muslim, propertied and Western-aligned. Their influence at home rests on letters, smuggled books and a myth of steppe freedom.

2.name: Alash aruağy
2.text:
The Spirit of Alash is the quiet heritage of the Alash Orda, the liberal Kazakh autonomy of 1917-1920 led by Alikhan Bukeikhanov, Akhmet Baitursynov and Mirzhakyp Dulatov, all of whom died in Stalin's purges. Their names are still banned in 1970, but philologists, historians and older teachers in Alma-Ata pass on their writings in private.

The circle dreams of constitutional rule, a Kazakh parliament, freedom of the press and an end to Russification, much as Bukeikhanov's Kadet allies once did. It looks with sympathy towards Western democracy but avoids open dissent. Its leverage lies in the universities, the Academy of Sciences and the Kazakh-language press, where every rehabilitation debate reopens the question of Alash.

3.name: Jer, adamğa tabyn!
3.text:
Earth, Bow to Man! takes its name from the 1961 poem with which Olzhas Suleimenov greeted Gagarin's flight from Baikonur. In 1970 Suleimenov is the star of a young, bilingual Kazakh intelligentsia of poets, film-makers and journalists who grew up in the Thaw and still believe that socialism can be humane and creative.

They want less censorship, more respect for the Kazakh language and history, honest discussion of the famine of the 1930s and a Communist Party that listens rather than commands. They do not challenge Soviet power or the Warsaw Pact. Their strength lies in culture: theatre premieres, literary journals, Kazakhfilm and the admiration of urban students.

4.name: Qazaqstan Kommunistik Partiyasy
4.text:
The Communist Party of Kazakhstan is the republican branch of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union and the sole legal party of the Kazakh SSR. Since December 1964 it has been led by First Secretary Dinmukhamed Kunaev, a mining engineer, close ally of Leonid Brezhnev and candidate member of the Soviet Politburo.

The party carries out Moscow's plan for grain, coal, metals and the space programme while quietly widening the room for Kazakh cadres. It is loyal to the USSR and hostile to Washington and Beijing alike after the 1969 border clashes. Its power rests on the nomenklatura, the obkom secretaries of every province and Kunaev's personal line to Brezhnev.

5.name: Temirtau köterilisi
5.text:
The Temirtau Uprising lives on among the young workers of the Karaganda metallurgical giant, where in August 1959 Komsomol volunteers living in tents without water rioted over food and pay until troops opened fire. A decade later the shock-construction hostels of Temirtau, Ekibastuz and Rudny still breed the same anger.

This milieu wants real workers' power: elected managers, equal pay, housing before prestige projects and the end of privileges for the apparatus. It quotes Lenin against the bureaucrats and has no love for either Moscow's planners or the West. Its leverage is the strike and the riot, in industrial towns the party cannot afford to see stop.

6.name: Karlagovskaya gvardiya
6.text:
The Karlag Old Guard are the former camp officers, NKVD veterans and Stalin-era cadres who stayed in Karaganda after the Karaganda Corrective Labour Camp was wound up in 1959. Many now sit in Russian-speaking city committees, mine administrations and police departments across northern Kazakhstan and welcome the end of Khrushchev's de-Stalinization.

They want iron discipline, a rehabilitation of Stalin's name, firm Russification and no concessions to Kazakh national feeling. They distrust Kunaev's indulgence of local clans and see China and America as twin enemies. Their leverage lies in the security organs, the old camp economy of the coal basin and allies in Moscow who share their nostalgia.

7.name: Qazaq KSR Memlekettik Qauipsizdik Komiteti
7.text:
The KGB of the Kazakh SSR is the republican arm of the Committee for State Security, subordinate to Yuri Andropov in Moscow and headquartered in Alma-Ata. After the 1969 border clashes with China at Zhalanashkol it is more powerful than ever, watching Uyghur refugees, the sealed nuclear and space zones and every hint of nationalism.

It stands for order without politics: secrecy, vigilance, informers in every institute and the border as a fortress. It answers to Moscow first and Kunaev second. Its leverage is information, the border troops of the Eastern District and the files it holds on every official in the republic.

8.name: Sürgün camaatı
8.text:
The Congregation of the Exiles gathers the Azerbaijani and Iranian Shia families deported to southern Kazakhstan from the Caucasian border zones in 1937-1938 and during the war. In 1970 they live in kolkhozes around Chimkent, Dzhambul and Alma-Ata, without a single registered Shia mosque, praying in homes and marking Muharram in private.

Its elders seek tolerance rather than power: the right to a prayer house, contact with the Spiritual Administration in Baku and permission to return to the Caucasus. They avoid politics and present themselves as loyal Soviet citizens. Their influence rests on tight family networks, trade at the bazaars and quiet links to relatives in Azerbaijan.

9.name: Näcäf müqallidläri
9.text:
The Followers of Najaf are a handful of older mullahs among the deported Azerbaijani and Iranian Shia of Kazakhstan who still follow the rulings of the great marja of Najaf, Muhsin al-Hakim, and keep secret ties to clerics in Iraq and Iran. They teach Persian and Arabic texts to a few pupils in the villages of the south.

They hold that only qualified jurists may guide the believers and reject both Soviet atheism and the state-approved clergy. Hostile to Moscow and suspicious of the Shah, they await a revival of Shia learning. Their leverage is small: spiritual authority within a closed community and the respect owed to the few who can still read the texts.

10.name: Orta Osiyo va Qozog'iston musulmonlari diniy boshqarmasi
10.english: Spiritual Administration of the Muslims of Central Asia and Kazakhstan
10.native_full: Orta Osiyo va Qozog'iston musulmonlari diniy boshqarmasi
10.text:
The Spiritual Administration of the Muslims of Central Asia and Kazakhstan is the state-recognised Muslim authority founded in Tashkent in 1943 and headed since 1957 by Mufti Ziyauddin Babakhanov. In Kazakhstan it acts through its qaziyat in Alma-Ata and a few dozen registered mosques, all under the eye of the Council for Religious Affairs.

It teaches a loyal, scholarly Hanafi Islam that condemns superstition, shrine cults and politics alike, and it serves Soviet diplomacy by hosting delegations from the Arab world. It accepts the USSR and attacks Western imperialism. Its leverage is legitimacy: the only legal imams, the Mir-i Arab madrasa graduates and the ear of Muslims abroad.
10.wiki: Spiritual Administration of the Muslims of Central Asia and Kazakhstan

11.name: Äziret Sultan muridteri
11.text:
The Murids of Hazret Sultan are unregistered mullahs, ishans and pilgrims gathered around the mausoleum of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi in the town of Turkestan, the holiest shrine of the Kazakhs. Soviet propaganda attacks them as parasites, and in 1970 they operate entirely underground among the cotton and rice villages of the Syr Darya.

They reject the Soviet state as infidel rule, dismiss the official muftiate as its servant and dream of restoring an Islamic order like that of the old khanates, with sharia in place of Soviet law. They hate Moscow and the West alike. Their leverage is pilgrimage, secret instruction and the deep piety of the southern villages.

12.name: Jädidter
12.text:
The Jadids are the heirs of the Muslim reform movement that, before 1917, founded new-method schools across the Kazakh steppe with the help of Tatar teachers and printers. In 1970 the tradition survives among Tatar and Kazakh families in Semipalatinsk, Petropavlovsk and Alma-Ata, where elderly teachers still pass on reformed Islamic learning at home.

They favour an educated, modern faith compatible with science, women's schooling and national culture, and see Islam as the moral backbone of a self-confident Kazakh society. They are cautious towards Soviet power and wary of Western materialism. Their leverage lies in schools, family libraries and intellectuals who blend Islamic ethics with enlightenment ideals.

13.name: Ūly jüz
13.text:
The Senior Horde Network is the web of patronage around First Secretary Dinmukhamed Kunaev, staffed heavily by cadres from the southern clans of the Senior Zhuz and from Kunaev's old colleagues in mining and the Academy of Sciences. Since 1964 it has quietly filled ministries, obkoms and institutes with loyal Kazakh officials.

It seeks stability, local control and a growing share of Moscow's investment for Alma-Ata, trading loyal plan fulfilment for freedom from interference. It has no ideology beyond self-preservation and stays aloof from bloc politics. Its leverage is personnel: appointments, flats, cars and Kunaev's friendship with Brezhnev, which shields it from Moscow's auditors.

14.name: Tselinniki
14.text:
The Virgin Landers are the directors of the giant grain sovkhozes created in northern Kazakhstan during the Virgin Lands campaign launched in 1954, when Leonid Brezhnev himself served in Alma-Ata. Based in Tselinograd, Kustanai, Kokchetav and Pavlodar, they manage millions of hectares of wheat and a largely Slavic workforce.

They want machinery, fertiliser, higher grain prices and protection from both erosion and Alma-Ata's interference, and they value practical results over ideology. They neither oppose Moscow nor look abroad. Their leverage is the harvest itself: the republic's billion poods of grain, their personal ties to Brezhnev's men and the veterans' prestige of the Tselina epic.

15.name: Ministerstvo srednego mashinostroyeniya SSSR
15.text:
The Ministry of Medium Machine Building, run since 1957 by Yefim Slavsky, is the secret empire behind the Soviet nuclear programme. In Kazakhstan it runs the Ulba plant in Ust-Kamenogorsk, uranium mines around Stepnogorsk, the fast-breeder reactor under construction at Shevchenko and, with the army, the Semipalatinsk test site.

It answers only to Moscow, builds closed cities with their own shops and salaries, and treats the republic's leaders as guests on its land. It serves the nuclear rivalry with the United States above all else. Its leverage is unmatched: limitless budgets, secrecy, the best engineers in the Union and direct access to the Politburo.

16.name: Kök bazar
16.text:
The Green Bazaar takes its name from the central market of Alma-Ata, where kolkhoz traders, speculators and shop managers run the republic's grey economy. Apples, mutton, Indian tea, jeans from Tashkent and deficit spare parts change hands at prices the planners never set, protected by bribes and kinship.

Its people want the freedom to buy, sell and keep the profit, lower taxes on private plots and an end to raids by the OBKhSS. They care little for ideology and admire Western goods more than Western politics. Their leverage is that every family, and many officials, depend on what only the bazaar can deliver.

17.name: Qazaq tabiğatty qorğau qoğamy
17.text:
The Kazakh Society for Nature Conservation is the republic's official voluntary nature-protection body, uniting biologists, teachers, hunters and schoolchildren. In 1970 it runs tree-planting campaigns and nature reserves, while its scientists note with alarm that the Aral Sea has begun to shrink as cotton irrigation drains the Syr Darya and Amu Darya.

Its members want stricter control of irrigation, protection of Lake Balkhash and the steppe from erosion, and, more quietly, honesty about the health of villages near the Semipalatinsk test site. It works within the Soviet system and avoids confrontation. Its leverage is scientific authority, the press and a growing public unease about the cost of gigantic projects.

18.name: Qazaqstan kasipodaqtar keñesi
18.english: Kazakh Republican Council of Trade Unions
18.text:
The Kazakh Republican Council of Trade Unions is the republic's branch of the All-Union Central Council of Trade Unions, organising miners, steelworkers, railwaymen and sovkhoz workers from Karaganda to Mangyshlak. In 1970 it is a transmission belt of the party, but its local committees handle housing, holidays and grievances for millions.

Within those limits it pushes for higher wages, safer mines, shorter hours and better social services, and it speaks the language of equality rather than of the plan. It is loyal to the Soviet order and anti-imperialist in rhetoric. Its leverage lies in the factory committees and in management's fear of another Temirtau.

19.name: Jas Tūlpar
19.text:
Zhas Tulpar was the society of Kazakh students in Moscow founded in 1963, with Murat Auezov, son of the writer Mukhtar Auezov, among its leading figures. Accused of nationalism, it was dissolved within a few years, yet in 1970 its former members are young scholars, writers and officials who keep in touch.

They see themselves as true Leninists who want a Kazakhstan that is socialist in content and Kazakh in form: native-language schooling, honest history, more Kazakh cadres and real republican sovereignty within the Union. They reject both Western capitalism and Russian chauvinism. Their leverage is a network of talented young people rising through the institutions.

20.name: Qazaq jeri
20.text:
Kazakh Land is the populist mood born in 1960-1961, when Zhumabek Tashenev, then chairman of the Kazakh Council of Ministers, refused Khrushchev's demand to hand the northern Virgin Lands provinces to Russia and was sacked for it. In 1970 Tashenev is a demoted provincial official, but his stand is told in every Kazakh village.

The current speaks for rural Kazakhs who feel outnumbered by Slavic settlers: the land must stay Kazakh, jobs and flats should go to locals, and Moscow's projects must not swallow pasture and graves. It distrusts both Russian officials and Western ideas. Its leverage is resentment, the village elders and the youth of the south.

21.name: Türkistan legiony
21.text:
The Turkistan Legion was the Wehrmacht formation raised from Central Asian prisoners of war in 1942, many of them Kazakhs, who fought for a German-sponsored Turkestan. Those who were repatriated served long Gulag sentences; others stayed in West Germany, Turkey or the United States. In 1970 the veterans are old men bound by secrecy and bitterness.

Their ideal remains an ethnically pure Turkic state, ruled by a strongman and purged of Russians and communists, an ideology learned in the camps of the Ostlegionen. They are fiercely anti-Soviet and look to any power that fights Moscow. Their leverage is negligible: émigré ties, private memories and a legend kept alive by Soviet propaganda itself.

22.name: Sredneaziatskiy voyennyy okrug
22.text:
The Central Asian Military District was re-established in 1969 with its headquarters in Alma-Ata, after the Sino-Soviet border fighting that culminated at Zhalanashkol in August. Commanded by General Nikolai Lyashchenko, it is rapidly filling the Kazakh frontier with motor rifle divisions, air bases and fortified areas.

The generals demand absolute priority for defence against China, unquestioned control of the border zones and resources for the garrisons, while the Strategic Rocket Forces guard Baikonur and its launch pads. They are loyal to the Soviet leadership but impatient with civilians. Their leverage is force itself and the conviction in Moscow that war with China is possible.

23.name: Aq süyek
23.text:
The White Bone Nobility are the families of the töre, the descendants of Genghis Khan who supplied the Kazakh khans, and of the qoja, the holy lineages, until the Russian Empire abolished the khanates. Dispossessed and persecuted after 1917, they survive in 1970 as respected but cautious families who still know their genealogies.

They cherish the memory of Abylai Khan and Kenesary Khan, the last to fight Russian rule, and imagine a Kazakhstan led again by a khan of noble blood. They are hostile to Soviet levelling but have no foreign patron. Their leverage is prestige: genealogy still matters at weddings, funerals and in the quiet calculations of the clans.
